class_id: a threshold constant is written in one unit and compared against a column stored in another, so every row lands in the same band
feature: any scoring, tiering, banding, alerting or gating rule whose literal thresholds were typed from how a human SAYS the quantity, while the column holds it in the unit the system STORES
symptom: a rule compares a stored value against literal thresholds a person wrote while thinking in display units — crore, thousands, MB, minutes, percent-as-0-to-100. The code type-checks, the arithmetic is valid, nothing throws, and no test fails if the fixtures were typed in the same wrong unit as the thresholds. But because real data is uniformly in the other unit and the gap is a fixed multiplier, EVERY row falls on the same side of every boundary. The output is a constant dressed as a calculation: a score that contributes no ranking, an alert that never fires or always fires, a tier everyone is in. It is not a wrong answer for some inputs, which is what testing usually looks for; it is the same answer for all of them, which reads as 'that component just isn't very discriminating'. The generic test is to feed the rule the LARGEST and the SMALLEST real stored values and assert the outputs DIFFER — a rule whose extremes agree is either unit-confused or dead. Fixture-level tests cannot find it, because the fixture and the threshold usually come from the same person's head on the same day.
first_seen: 2026-09-21 -- IPODhan item 11 (OD-20), two files with the identical defect. `web/lib/services/ipo-scoring-realtime.ts` scored issue size against 1000/500/100 and `web/lib/utils/rating-calculator.ts` against 1000/500/100 -- both CRORE figures -- while `ipos.issue_size` is stored in RUPEES. Measured read-only on ipodhan_staging: 314 of 366 rows hold a rupee-shaped value (>= 1e7), and the SMALLEST genuine row (PIYUSH, Rs0.70 Cr = 7,007,320 rupees) is still 7,007x the top threshold -- so the largest IPO on the site (NSE, Rs26,579.64 Cr) and the smallest scored IDENTICALLY. Both terms were constant across every IPO. The existing unit tests passed throughout because their fixtures were typed in crore (`issueSize: 2500, // Rs2500 Cr`) -- the same confusion as the code, so they agreed with it; the shared `mockIPOData` used 1500, meaning every OTHER test in that file was silently exercising the bottom band. `rating-calculator.ts` had NO test at all, which is why its half stayed 'documented, not fixed' (F-77) while the twin was tracked (F-95). Reached from a live API route (`app/api/ipos/[slug]/rating/route.ts`) and `scripts/calculate-ratings.ts`. A shared `RUPEES_PER_CRORE` constant already existed in `web/lib/utils.ts`, carrying a comment that says 'one calc treated it as crores' -- the class had been SEEN and the constant created, without the two call sites being changed.
fix_prs: convert at the READ using the already-shared constant (`value / RUPEES_PER_CRORE`) rather than restating the thresholds in rupees -- OD-20 makes crore the stored unit, so the crore-denominated comparison is the one that survives the coming migration and the rupee-denominated one would have to be undone. Failing tests first, written from REAL stored values rather than fixtures: 3 red on the scoring service (every case returned the maximum 0.75, including a Rs0.70 Cr IPO) and 5 red on the rating calculator (`calculateMarketScore` exported for the purpose, since an untested private function is what let F-77 survive). Then the pre-existing fixtures were corrected to rupees, because leaving them would have re-encoded the defect in the test suite. Both mutants killed by reverting the division (8 failed).
detection_check: none yet. The cheap general check is a property test per banding rule: feed it the minimum and maximum values actually present in its source column and FAIL if the outputs are equal. That catches unit confusion, an inverted comparison and a dead branch with one assertion, needs no knowledge of the intended units, and would have fired on both of these the day they were written. A schema-level companion: every numeric column carries its unit in a machine-readable ruling (this repo has one -- `docs/design/probes/amount-columns.mjs`), and any literal compared against that column is checked against the ruling.
